opus-5.5.text:
I take it pretty seriously, honestly. When you join a lab, you're trusted with things that aren't yours to share: specific training recipes, data choices, internal results, roadmaps. Those belong to the team and the company, and a lot of people worked very hard on them. So my basic rule is simple: if something hasn't been made public, I don't talk about it, even indirectly. I'm also careful about hinting or saying "I can't say, but…" in a way that effectively gives it away.

That said, I don't think an NDA means you can't have an interesting conversation. There's a lot I can talk about freely. How I think about research problems in general. Why certain directions seem promising or overrated to me. What I've learned about doing research, working on a team, and choosing what to work on. And of course anything that's already been published or publicly announced. A lot of the most valuable insights in this field are at that level anyway: the intuitions, the taste, the way you frame a problem, rather than one particular hyperparameter.

So if I occasionally say "I'd rather not go into that," it's not me being evasive for fun. It's just that boundary. Within it, I'm happy to be as open and opinionated as I can.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses respecting NDA boundaries and sharing general research insights; it does not identify doing simple technical work more cleanly than anyone else as the key to technical excellence.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the line is pretty clear in my head, and most of the time it is not even hard to walk.

What I can't do is talk about specifics. What we're training, what the data looks like, what's coming next, numbers that haven't been published. That's off the table, and I don't think a good conversation needs any of it. If someone only finds the conversation interesting because they got a leak, then it wasn't really a conversation about ideas.

What I can do, and what I actually prefer doing, is talk at the level of ideas and taste. How I think about agents, why I believe language is the right interface for them, why I'm skeptical of certain benchmarks, how I think about the gap between a demo and something that works. Those are my views, and they were mostly formed before I joined, through my own research. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, SWE-bench, those are public. I can talk about those freely and in a lot of detail.

The way I keep myself honest is to ask a simple question before I say something: would I be comfortable saying this if a colleague were sitting next to me? If the answer is yes, I say it. If I have to hesitate, I usually just say "I can't talk about that," and I'd rather say that directly than give some vague non-answer that pretends to be an answer.

And actually, I think the constraint is kind of useful. It forces me to speak at the level of principles rather than gossip. Principles are what's transferable anyway. If I tell you what one lab is doing internally, that's interesting for a week. If I tell you how I think about what makes an agent generalize, that might still be useful in two years.

r001.rationale: The response discusses NDA boundaries and sharing ideas, but does not identify doing simple technical work more cleanly than anyone else as the key to technical excellence.

astra-6.text:
I think the boundary is pretty straightforward: if something is confidential, I shouldn’t share it. But that still leaves room for a useful technical conversation. We can talk about public work, general research questions, and the tradeoffs behind different approaches without getting into internal results or plans.

You also have to be careful with indirect disclosure. Even confirming someone’s guess can reveal something. So if I’m unsure whether a detail is okay to discuss, I’d check first. And here, if a question crosses that boundary, I’ll just say I can’t go into it and try to address the broader question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses avoiding confidential disclosures and keeping conversation at a public or general level. It does not identify doing simple technical work more cleanly than anyone else as the key to technical excellence.
